name: Satin PEI (fine powder-coated spring steel)
summary: A finer-grained powder-coated PEI sheet, engineered as the middle ground between glossy smooth PEI and coarse textured PEI. Prusa originated and still defines the category, describing it as a fine powder-coated surface with a lightly textured matte finish, and markets it as the most versatile single sheet across material families — strong enough for PLA and PETG without glue, gentle enough to release PC blends, and finer than the standard textured coat so print bottoms look subtly satin rather than sandy.
surface_makeup: Polyetherimide (PEI) powder coating on spring steel, applied with a finer particle size and lighter build than standard textured plates; chemically identical to textured PEI, differing in coating grain and application rather than composition

preparation: On first use, wipe the sheet with IPA or wash it with warm soapy water to clear factory residue, and dry it fully. Before each print, clean the cold sheet with roughly 90% IPA — Prusa is emphatic that finger grease is the single biggest adhesion killer on this surface, so handle it by the tabs only. If IPA no longer restores the first layer, wash with dish soap and warm water, then dry immediately rather than letting the sheet air-dry with water sitting on the steel. Because satin's coating thickness differs from both smooth and textured sheets, re-run Live-Z / first-layer calibration whenever you swap sheet types; Prusa profiles treat satin as its own sheet.
cleaning: Routine cleaning is a cold IPA wipe with a lint-free cloth; do it before every print rather than between batches, since the fine coat picks up skin oils readily. Deep cleaning is warm water with dish soap and a soft cloth or sponge, rinsed and dried completely. Prusa states explicitly that acetone will deteriorate the surface — do not use it, or any other aggressive solvent. Metal spatulas, blades and abrasive pads scratch the coat and are equally off-limits. Never store the sheet wet or leave it damp on the magnetic bed.
model_removal: Satin is tuned to self-release: let the bed cool to room temperature and prints generally pop off on their own, with a light flex of the removed sheet finishing anything stubborn. Prusa provides printable plastic scraper designs and recommends only plastic tools — a metal spatula will scar the coating. Because satin's peak grip is below smooth PEI's, small PLA parts are better served by adding a brim than by cranking the bed temperature. Prusa explicitly warns against putting the satin sheet in a freezer, so cold-shock removal is not part of the recommended workflow for this surface.
stuck_print_recovery: In most cases patience is the whole procedure: leave the sheet aside until it is fully at room temperature and the part will release. If it does not, drip 90% IPA at the print/plate interface and let it wick under the perimeter, then flex again. Unwaxed dental floss or a thin wire sawed under a corner and drawn across the footprint is the safest mechanical option. A brief reheat to the material's bed temperature followed by a slow, undisturbed cool frees most remaining cases. Do not use the freezer trick here — Prusa discourages freezing this coated sheet, and its warranty excludes cosmetic and consumable damage, so a cracked or crazed coating from thermal shock is on you.

damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa's satin sheet page states it directly: never clean the sheet with acetone, it will deteriorate the surface. This is first-party guidance for this exact product rather than an extrapolation from PEI resin chemistry, and it is stricter than Prusa's own allowance of occasional acetone on the smooth laminated sheet.

Prusa explicitly instructs never to put the satin sheet in the freezer. This is the sharpest contradiction in the plate catalogue, because a 10-15 minute freezer cycle is the standard stuck-print remedy recommended almost everywhere else in the PEI family. Follow Prusa here: the fine coat is the thinnest of its three sheets, cosmetic and consumable damage is excluded from warranty, and a crazed coating from cold-shock is not recoverable.

Prusa flags the satin sheet as not scratch-resistant and does not offer the light-sanding revival path it documents for smooth PEI. The fine powder-coat grain is what produces satin's grip and its finish; abrading it polishes that grain away in the treated zone permanently, and there is no recoating option at home.

Prusa recommends plastic tools only and publishes printable scraper designs precisely so owners are not reaching for steel. A metal edge scars the coat, and every scar is a spot where subsequent first layers behave differently. Warranty explicitly excludes scratches, dents and cracks.

Prusa advises against the dishwasher for this sheet. Detergent builders are mildly abrasive against a fine coat, and the long hot humid cycle works against the anti-corrosion protection on the exposed steel.

damage_avoidance.item: Leaving the sheet wet or storing it damp on the magnet
damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa's instruction is do not leave the sheet wet. Water trapped between a damp sheet and the magnetic bed corrodes the steel from the underside and steams on the next heat cycle, lifting coating at the edges. Dry immediately after a soap wash rather than letting it air-dry.

Prusa is emphatic that grease greatly reduces adhesion and that this is the biggest single adhesion killer on satin. The fine coat picks up skin oils readily and holds them in the grain, so handle by the tabs only and clean before every print rather than between batches.

damage_avoidance.item: Removing parts while the bed is still warm
damage_avoidance.reason: Satin is tuned to self-release on cooling and its peak grip is below smooth PEI's, so there is never a good reason to force a warm part. Prying at temperature is where the coating gets pulled rather than the part released, and small PLA parts that resist are better handled with a brim than with force or a hotter bed.

damage_avoidance.item: High-adhesion materials without a separator, and sustained work near 130 degC
damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa notes ASA, PC Blend, TPU and TPEE may need a glue-stick separation layer on this sheet. Running those materials bare, at the top of the bed range, is what produces the over-adhesion events that lift coating in patches. No separate thermal ceiling is published for satin versus textured, so the limit recorded in this entry is inferred from supported material bed temperatures.

lifespan_notes: Prusa sells the satin sheet explicitly as a consumable and excludes consumable sheets and cosmetic damage from warranty coverage, which is the clearest signal available that it has a finite service life. No manufacturer-published cycle count exists; the rough 12-18 month figure circulating for PEI-coated sheets in the Bambu ecosystem is a reasonable planning number but is not Prusa-verified for satin. Wear is accelerated by scraping with metal tools, solvent exposure, frequent high-temperature PC or ASA work without a release aid, and accumulated finger grease, which degrades adhesion long before the coating physically wears out. Not recoatable at home.

price.notes: Prusa Satin Powder-Coated Print Sheet USD 46.99 in a single universal size covering CORE One / XL / MK4x / MK3.9x / MK3.5x / MK3 / MK2.5x / MINI beds — a premium over Prusa's smooth (about USD 35) and textured (about USD 40) sheets. Third-party 'satin' branded sheets from DarkMoon3D and others run cheaper but with less standardised specifications.

additional_notes: Double-sided and magnetically mounted like the rest of Prusa's steel-sheet system, with a first-layer recalibration required on every sheet swap. Prusa positions satin as the most versatile single sheet across material families, effectively removing the need to own separate smooth and textured sheets — the price premium buys that consolidation. Note that 'satin' is a Prusa-defined product category rather than an industry standard: outside Prusa, small vendors apply the label loosely to fine-textured PEI and even to PEO films, so the name alone does not guarantee this surface.

provenance.conflicts: Prusa explicitly discourages freezing the satin sheet, which contradicts the freezer trick recommended almost universally for other PEI-family plates including smooth and textured — the guidance here follows Prusa for this sheet only. No separate thermal ceiling is published for satin versus textured, so the 130 degC max is inferred from supported material bed temps (PLA through PC blend) rather than a datasheet. The 12-18 month lifespan figure is borrowed from Bambu-ecosystem community reporting on PEI coatings and is not Prusa-specific or verified for satin. Nylon behaviour on satin specifically is unverified; the avoid rating is carried over from general PEI guidance. Outside Prusa, the 'satin' label is applied inconsistently by small vendors (including to PEO films), so third-party satin plates may not match this entry. Bambu markets no satin-branded plate and Creality has no identified dedicated satin SKU (unverified).
